00-introduction.heading: Where this manual comes from
00-introduction.caption: Scenes from the handbook's project gardens: maize, fruit, mulched beds, a home run on solar power and a harvest of vegetables.

02-planning-your-farm.heading: Step 1: Site assessment
02-planning-your-farm.caption: A base map: an aerial photo of the property with contour lines, the buildings and a north arrow. Map what is already there before you plan anything new.

02-planning-your-farm.heading: Step 1: Site assessment
02-planning-your-farm.caption: A family draws their farm plan together. Plan on paper first: a mistake on paper costs nothing to fix.

02-planning-your-farm.heading: Step 2: Zone planning
02-planning-your-farm.caption: The same property divided into zones, from the home (Zone 0) out to the wild area (Zone 5). The places you visit every day are closest to the house.

02-planning-your-farm.heading: Step 2: Zone planning
02-planning-your-farm.caption: Zones as rings around the home: the house is Zone 0, and each zone further out is visited less often.

02-planning-your-farm.heading: Step 3: Slope planning
02-planning-your-farm.caption: Slope planning: water stored high up, trees on the steep upper slope, the house and gardens lower down, and greywater flowing on down to trees.

03-sector-planning.heading: Drawing a sector map
03-sector-planning.caption: A sector map of the same property: hot and cold winds, fire risk, the best view and cold air flowing downhill at night. The small inset shows the sun's path across the north.

03-sector-planning.heading: Finding north
03-sector-planning.caption: Finding north with a compass. In South Africa the needle points about 20 to 28 degrees west of true north.

03-sector-planning.heading: Sunlight
03-sector-planning.caption: The sun is in the north: high in the summer sky and low in winter, so winter shadows are much longer.

03-sector-planning.heading: Frost
03-sector-planning.caption: On still, clear nights cold air flows downhill and settles in low places. Leave a gap on the downhill side of a hedge so it can drain away.

04-vegetable-and-staple-crops.heading: 1. The kitchen garden (Zone 1)
04-vegetable-and-staple-crops.caption: A kitchen garden right beside the house, under a shade-net frame. It is the garden you pass many times a day (Zone 1).

04-vegetable-and-staple-crops.heading: 1. The kitchen garden (Zone 1)
04-vegetable-and-staple-crops.caption: A mandala garden: beds edged with timber offcuts curve around a central sitting place. A kitchen garden can be useful and beautiful.

04-vegetable-and-staple-crops.heading: 1. The kitchen garden (Zone 1)
04-vegetable-and-staple-crops.caption: Keyhole beds edged with recycled plastic strip, with stone paths and drip irrigation. You can reach every plant from the path.

04-vegetable-and-staple-crops.heading: 2. The vegetable garden (Zone 2)
04-vegetable-and-staple-crops.caption: Stone-edged vegetable beds of spinach and beetroot inside a fence. The paths let you work without stepping on the beds.

04-vegetable-and-staple-crops.heading: 2. The vegetable garden (Zone 2)
04-vegetable-and-staple-crops.caption: A home vegetable garden with mulched rows of cabbage, a short walk from the house (Zone 2).

04-vegetable-and-staple-crops.heading: 3. Small-scale commercial vegetable farming (Zone 3)
04-vegetable-and-staple-crops.caption: A market garden: long rows of one crop each, here green and red cabbage, make planting, weeding and harvesting quick.

04-vegetable-and-staple-crops.heading: 3. Small-scale commercial vegetable farming (Zone 3)
04-vegetable-and-staple-crops.caption: Two market-garden blocks seen from above. Beds of the same size make it easy to plan how much to plant and sell.

04-vegetable-and-staple-crops.heading: 4. The staple garden (Zone 3)
04-vegetable-and-staple-crops.caption: A tall, healthy stand of maize in a staple garden. Staple crops need a lot of space, so they go in Zone 3.

05-animal-systems.heading: Place animals where they work for you
05-animal-systems.caption: A chicken's needs, products and behaviours: what it needs (food, water, shelter, grit, dust), what it gives (eggs, meat, manure, feathers) and what it does by nature (scratching, pecking).

05-animal-systems.heading: Animal tractors
05-animal-systems.caption: Movable poultry pens (animal tractors) on grass. Move them every few days so the birds get fresh ground and the grass can recover.

05-animal-systems.heading: Animal tractors
05-animal-systems.caption: An A-frame chicken tractor: a light wooden frame with wire mesh, a tin roof for shade and rain, and a drinker inside.

05-animal-systems.heading: Animal tractors
05-animal-systems.caption: A solar energiser powers movable electric netting around a poultry run: an open animal tractor that you can shift across the land.

05-animal-systems.heading: Pigs
05-animal-systems.caption: Young pigs eating spoiled apricots. Pigs turn fallen and spoiled fruit into meat and manure.

05-animal-systems.heading: Pigs
05-animal-systems.caption: A pig tractor: pigs graze inside an electric fence powered by a small solar panel, with a simple shelter for shade.

05-animal-systems.heading: Pigs
05-animal-systems.caption: The ground after the pigs have moved on: they have rooted out the grass and turned the soil, ready for planting.

05-animal-systems.heading: Ducks
05-animal-systems.caption: Muscovy ducks resting in the shade. They help control pests, graze grass and are much quieter than other ducks.

05-animal-systems.heading: Bees
05-animal-systems.caption: A wooden beehive raised on a stack of old tyres: level, firm and off the damp ground.

06-tree-systems.heading: Food forests
06-tree-systems.caption: A subtropical food forest in Durban, seen from above: bananas, a young fruit tree, shrubs and groundcover, with no bare soil.

06-tree-systems.heading: Designing a food forest
06-tree-systems.caption: Quinces: a very frost-hardy fruit for jam and cooking, well suited to cold Highveld and Lesotho winters.

06-tree-systems.heading: Designing a food forest
06-tree-systems.caption: A young peach. Choose a peach variety that matches the winter cold where you live.

06-tree-systems.heading: Designing a food forest
06-tree-systems.caption: A young apple. Apples need cold winters; in warmer areas choose low-chill varieties.

06-tree-systems.heading: Planting a food forest
06-tree-systems.caption: Mixed cowpea and bean seed, ready to sow as a legume groundcover between young trees.

06-tree-systems.heading: Planting a food forest
06-tree-systems.caption: Planting basins dug and ready, with the young trees waiting beside them. Dig all the holes and basins before you plant.

06-tree-systems.heading: Planting a food forest
06-tree-systems.caption: A young lemon tree ringed by pigeon pea. The nitrogen fixers are cut back often and left on the ground as mulch (chop and drop).

06-tree-systems.heading: The layers of a food forest
06-tree-systems.caption: The seven layers of a food forest planted along a swale: tall trees, small trees, shrubs, herbs, roots, groundcover and climbers.

06-tree-systems.heading: The layers of a food forest
06-tree-systems.caption: Freshly dug turmeric: a crop for the root layer of a warm, frost-free food forest.

06-tree-systems.heading: Windbreaks
06-tree-systems.caption: Wild dagga (Leonotis leonurus): a fast-growing indigenous windbreak shrub whose orange flowers feed sunbirds.

06-tree-systems.heading: Windbreaks
06-tree-systems.caption: A windbreak of several rows of indigenous trees and shrubs, planted across the damaging wind and kept away from the north side of the garden.

06-tree-systems.heading: Planting a tree
06-tree-systems.caption: A planting hole two to three times as wide as the root ball, with the topsoil and subsoil kept in separate heaps and the stake knocked in first.

06-tree-systems.heading: Planting a tree
06-tree-systems.caption: Tying a young tree to its stake. Use a soft tie in a loose figure of eight so the stem can still move a little.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: What earthworks can do
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: An earthworks plan for a whole property: swales, basins and a pond catch runoff from the top of the land to the bottom, each with a safe overflow.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: What earthworks can do
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: A swale full of runoff from a nearby driveway. The water soaks into the soil slowly instead of running away.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: What earthworks can do
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: A long swale being dug by TLB, with a survey staff to check the level. Get experienced advice before any large machine earthworks.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Harvesting and storing rainwater
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: A recycled drum under a roof downpipe, with a tap near the bottom: a cheap way to start harvesting rainwater. Keep it covered.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Harvesting and storing rainwater
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: Three tanks joined by a pipe at the base, so they fill and empty together.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Infiltration basins
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: Stone-lined channels lead runoff into infiltration basins around young trees, watering them after every rain.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Ponds and dams
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: A runoff dam at the top of a property catches water flowing down the valley. Dams have legal rules in South Africa.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Ponds and dams
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: Digging a runoff pond with a TLB. Keep people well away from a working machine, and slope the sides of the hole.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Ponds and dams
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: The same pond, lined with plastic, three weeks later after 45 mm of rain. Fence ponds so that children cannot get in.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Sand dams
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: How a sand dam works: a concrete wall is built on bedrock across a dry river bed. Sand builds up behind it and holds water that the sun cannot dry up.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Sand dams
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: A sand dam across a river bed at a community centre in Lesotho.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Swales
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: An A-frame level: a string with a weight hangs from the top. When the string crosses the centre mark, both legs stand at the same height.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Swales
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: Pegging out a contour line with an A-frame. Each new peg is at the same height as the one before.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Swales
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: Digging a swale by hand along the pegged contour. The soil is piled on the downhill side to make the berm.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Swales
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: A planted swale and berm: amadumbe in the moist ditch, with lemongrass, sweet potato and pigeon pea on the berm.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Preparing the ground
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: A small vegetable garden prepared by hand by a team of volunteers. With many hands, digging goes quickly.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Preparing the ground
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: A two-wheel tractor: small enough for a smallholding, it can plough, rotavate and pull a planter.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Preparing the ground
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: Black plastic held down with bales and sandbags. Left for some weeks, it kills the grass so that beds can be made without digging.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Forming growing beds for vegetables
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: Beds pegged out along the contour on a slope, with the soil pulled downhill to make each bed level.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Forming growing beds for vegetables
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: Double-reach beds edged with stones and filled with good topsoil. Each bed is narrow enough to reach the middle from both sides.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Forming growing beds for vegetables
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: A pit bed (banana circle) lined with cardboard and filled with organic matter, being watered. The plants go around the rim.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Irrigation
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: Hand watering under shade cloth. Water the soil at the base of the plants, not the leaves.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Irrigation
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: Bottle irrigation: an upturned bottle buried beside the plants lets water seep slowly into the roots.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Irrigation
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: Drip irrigation: the drip line runs past the base of each pepper plant and wets only the soil around its roots.

07-earthworks-and-water.heading: Using greywater for irrigation
07-earthworks-and-water.caption: A greywater drum: kitchen water runs through a filter box (grease trap) and on to a mulched swale. Let it flow on the same day; stored greywater goes bad.

08-soil.heading: The layers of the soil
08-soil.caption: The layers of the soil: dark topsoil full of roots and life, lighter subsoil below, and stones and rock at the bottom.

08-soil.heading: Testing your soil
08-soil.caption: The jar test: shake soil with water in a clear jar, let it settle for a day, then read the layers of sand, silt and clay.

08-soil.heading: Caring for your soil
08-soil.caption: A young pumpkin-family seedling growing through straw mulch. The mulch keeps the soil covered, cool and moist.

08-soil.heading: Way 2: Animal manure
08-soil.caption: Spreading manure on freshly cut, moist grass: the first layer of a sheet-mulched bed.

08-soil.heading: Way 3: Mulch
08-soil.caption: Sheet mulching: cardboard laid over the grass and covered with compost. The cardboard smothers the grass and then rots away.

08-soil.heading: Way 3: Mulch
08-soil.caption: Planting seedlings through a thick layer of straw into the finished sheet-mulched bed.

08-soil.heading: Way 4: Compost
08-soil.caption: Building a compost heap on a base of sticks, which lets air in from below.

08-soil.heading: Way 4: Compost
08-soil.caption: Watering each layer as the compost heap is built. Keep it about as damp as a wrung-out sponge.

08-soil.heading: Way 5: Earthworms and worm farming
08-soil.caption: Red wigglers: the small compost worms used in a worm farm. They are a different kind from ordinary garden earthworms.

08-soil.heading: Way 5: Earthworms and worm farming
08-soil.caption: An old bath on bricks used as a worm farm, with a hessian cover to keep it dark and moist.

08-soil.heading: Way 5: Earthworms and worm farming
08-soil.caption: A stacking worm farm: the worms move up into the top tray of fresh food, and worm tea drains out at the bottom.

09-balanced-ecology.heading: Food chains and the ecological pyramid
09-balanced-ecology.caption: The ecological pyramid: many plants at the base, fewer plant-eaters above them, fewer predators again, and only a few top predators such as owls.

09-balanced-ecology.heading: Succession
09-balanced-ecology.caption: A dense cowpea groundcover. As a pioneer legume it covers bare soil, feeds it with nitrogen and gives food as well.

09-balanced-ecology.heading: Succession
09-balanced-ecology.caption: Pioneers first: pigeon pea and indigenous sweet thorn growing between young fruit trees to feed the soil.

09-balanced-ecology.heading: Habitat
09-balanced-ecology.caption: Filling a small wildlife pond made from an old tyre, a blanket and plastic, edged with stones. Frogs and dragonflies soon move in.

09-balanced-ecology.heading: Habitat
09-balanced-ecology.caption: A barn owl box on a pole at least 3 m above the ground. A family of barn owls can eat 1 000 or more rodents a year.

10-natural-pest-control.heading: Companion planting
10-natural-pest-control.caption: Cabbages with marigolds, nasturtiums and borage between them. The mixed flowers feed useful insects and help hide the cabbages from pests.

10-natural-pest-control.heading: Companion planting
10-natural-pest-control.caption: Nasturtium as a trap crop: aphids gather on its leaves instead of on the cabbages. Pick the infested leaves and feed them to the chickens.

10-natural-pest-control.heading: Good and poor neighbours
10-natural-pest-control.caption: Onions planted along the edge of a carrot bed: good neighbours in the garden.

11-home-and-appropriate-technology.heading: Design the house for the sun
11-home-and-appropriate-technology.caption: A stone-and-cob building at a community centre in Lesotho, with solar panels and a roof vent: a home designed for the sun.

11-home-and-appropriate-technology.heading: Solar energy
11-home-and-appropriate-technology.caption: Two small solar panels on a tin roof: enough for LED lights and charging phones.

11-home-and-appropriate-technology.heading: Solar energy
11-home-and-appropriate-technology.caption: An evacuated-tube solar geyser on a roof. Like solar panels, it should face north.

11-home-and-appropriate-technology.heading: Solar energy
11-home-and-appropriate-technology.caption: A box solar cooker with a pot of stew. Use thick gloves: the pot and the box get very hot.

11-home-and-appropriate-technology.heading: Drying food with the sun
11-home-and-appropriate-technology.caption: Halved fruit drying on corrugated iron. Dry food off the ground, cover it with netting against flies and bring it in at night.

11-home-and-appropriate-technology.heading: Drying food with the sun
11-home-and-appropriate-technology.caption: A solar dryer with a glass lid: food dries faster and stays clean, safe from flies and dust.

11-home-and-appropriate-technology.heading: Heat-retention cooking: the wonder bag
11-home-and-appropriate-technology.caption: A wonder bag. Bring the pot to the boil on the stove, then put it in the bag to finish cooking without more fuel.

11-home-and-appropriate-technology.heading: Rocket stoves
11-home-and-appropriate-technology.caption: A rocket stove cut away to show inside: sticks burn at the base of a short, insulated chimney, so the fire is hot and uses little wood.

11-home-and-appropriate-technology.heading: Biogas digesters
11-home-and-appropriate-technology.caption: How a household biogas digester works: manure and food waste go in, gas flows to the kitchen stove, and the slurry goes to the garden.

11-home-and-appropriate-technology.heading: Biogas digesters
11-home-and-appropriate-technology.caption: Building a household biogas digester in Lesotho: the tank sits in a block-lined pit. Never work alone in a pit.

11-home-and-appropriate-technology.heading: Biogas digesters
11-home-and-appropriate-technology.caption: A finished household biogas digester, with the gas pipe running to the kitchen. Biogas can explode: keep flames away from leaks and let fresh air in.
